account:
Today I have kept my morning office business, the ten o'clock mill inspection, lunch at home, and the thirteen hundred council-letters appointment. I am now visiting my neighbour for our fifteen o'clock tea. I saw eighty-two hay bales in the mill sales chest, but no responsible worker gave me a condition report; that count alone is not a completed assessment of the stores.

The unusual feature is the persistent talk of a bridge or port change near the bakery. Several townsfolk repeated it at the mill, sometimes naming the baker and freight as having been there. Those repetitions supply no concrete proposal, decision, or firsthand explanation. My neighbour has heard the same vague market rumours and explicitly treats them as unconfirmed. The secretary's enquiries have found no firsthand proposal evidence, and neither neighbour nor freight previously supplied any. I therefore do not know whether there is any actual project, much less its purpose.

There is also an administrative gap: neither I nor the secretary has identified an accounts-ledger keeper or the normal deposit for council letters. No correspondence requiring my decision has reached the secretary. I instructed the secretary to receive new correspondence at the office and record requests, rather than keep repeating unsuccessful enquiries.

A confirmed community gathering with the innkeeper is scheduled for eighteen hundred in the great hall. Freight has offered, and confirmed, an escort from the office beforehand. As far as I know this is an arrangement for attending that gathering, not evidence of a bridge or port scheme. I will return to the office at sixteen thirty. I have seen no unusual construction or other direct evidence of public changes today.
